cards.text: A letter just came in, friend, from Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ. Servant FIRST, then apostle, so the man had the big title and still led with the apron. He's writing to people who received their faith through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ.

cards.question: Peter tells his readers they received a faith as ___ as ours.

cards.text: Then comes his greeting: "Grace and peace be multiplied to you…" MULTIPLIED, friend, like a batch that doubles every time you open the oven, and I would trade my mustache for that oven… okay, not the mustache, I'd have nothing left to hold the spatula.

cards.question: Peter wants grace and peace multiplied to his readers. Through what?

answers.text: The knowledge of God and of Jesus
The strength of their own effort

cards.text: Now Peter talks about what God's divine power has given us for life and godliness. Hold onto your apron, friend.

cards.question: How much of what we need for life and godliness has God's divine power given us?

answers.text: Most of it with the rest on us

cards.text: And it all comes through the knowledge of Him, the One who called us by His own glory and excellence. That word "knowledge" again, friend, two verses in a row.
Through these, He has given us His "precious and magnificent promises". MAGNIFICENT, friend, and nobody has ever said that about "I'll call you right back."

cards.question: Peter says God gave these precious promises for a reason. What is it?

answers.text: So they may share in the divine nature
So they may never face hard times again
So they may be rewarded with great riches

cards.question: Peter says these believers are still waiting to escape the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.

cards.text: Because of all God has given them, Peter writes, "For this very reason, make every effort…" Not snooze-button effort, friend, not "I'll start Monday" effort, EVERY effort.

cards.question: Peter tells his readers to make every effort to add to something they already have. What is it?

cards.text: To their faith, Peter says, add virtue.

cards.question: Peter says that once they add virtue to their faith, they're done adding.

cards.text: Not even close, friend. To virtue add knowledge, then self-control, perseverance, godliness and brotherly kindness, and that box is getting so tall I need the WHOLE mustache just to carry it.

cards.question: Peter's list climbs one quality at a time. What's the last one he adds, right on top of brotherly kindness?

cards.text: So why stack all that? Peter says if they have these qualities and keep growing in them, it makes a real difference in how they know our Lord Jesus Christ.

cards.question: If they keep growing in these qualities, those qualities will keep them from being ineffective and ___ in their knowledge of Jesus.

cards.text: But someone missing these traits, Peter says, is "nearsighted to the point of blindness". That's me reading a recipe card, friend: I can see my own mustache and NOTHING past it.

cards.question: Peter says the person missing these traits has forgotten something. What?

answers.text: That he was cleansed from his past sins
That he once promised to follow God
That he still has work to finish

cards.text: So Peter brings it home and calls them brothers: strive to make your calling and election sure. Not "I THINK I turned the oven off" sure, friend, SURE sure.

cards.question: Peter says if they practice these things, they will ___ stumble.
Peter ends with what's waiting for them. What kind of welcome will they receive into the eternal kingdom of Jesus?

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess Peter's exact word ("precious") with no setup that points to it. Nothing on card 1 lets the baker reason toward "precious" over "new", so the card tests wording they haven't seen, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card runs well past 2 sentences. It is one long run-on joined with commas and ellipses, and it packs in the greeting quote, the doubling-batch comparison, the trade-my-mustache line and the take-back about the spatula. That is more than two beats.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: Three of the walkthrough's jokes are built on the mustache (stop 1 card 3, stop 2 card 5, stop 2 card 9). That makes the mustache his main joke source in this lesson.

rule.text: The mustache is a fact about him, not his main source of jokes.

findings.problem: The setup line "Hold onto your apron, friend" signals that the answer is something big. That rules out "Just enough to get started" and "Most of it with the rest on us" before the baker reasons about card 6.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The right answer "So they may share in the divine nature" is the only one in Bible-sounding language. "Never face hard times again" and "rewarded with great riches" read as plain modern guesses, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Most of stop 1's choice cards are pure discovery. Card 4 (through what grace and peace are multiplied), card 9 (the reason for the promises) and card 10 (whether they have already escaped corruption) get no story-card context to reason from. Only card 6 has any setup, so most of the stop comes down to luck.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The right answer (False: they aren't done after virtue) rests only on 2 Peter 1:5 ("and to virtue, knowledge"), but the card cites 2 Peter 1:5-7.

rule.text: A choice card cites only the verses of its right answer.
